sections.section_title: Timothy Joins the Mission and the Decrees Are Delivered
sections.summary: Paul circumcises Timothy (a man of Jewish maternal lineage) for practical reasons, delivers the Jerusalem Council's decrees to the churches, and the churches are strengthened in the faith and increase in numbers daily.

sections.section_title: The Spirit Redirects the Mission to Macedonia
sections.summary: The Holy Spirit forbids Paul from speaking in Asia, and the Spirit of Jesus blocks entry into Bithynia; a vision of a Macedonian man appealing for help leads Paul and companions to conclude that God has called them to preach the gospel in Macedonia -- the 'we' narrative begins as the author joins the party at Troas.

sections.section_title: Philippi and the Conversion of Lydia
sections.summary: At a riverside gathering in Philippi, Lydia -- a God-fearing businesswoman from Thyatira -- hears Paul speak, and 'the Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said'; she and her household are baptized and she prevails upon the missionaries to stay at her house.
sections.relevance: The phrase 'the Lord opened her heart' (ho kyrios dienoixen ten kardian) attributes Lydia's receptivity to divine initiative. The neutral reading notes that 'her hearing is made possible by the Lord's prior action of opening her heart' and that 'the divine action enables human response; it does not replace it.' If the Lord must open the heart for faith to occur, this raises the question of whether what God initiates by sovereign action might also be sustained by sovereign action. However, the text addresses only the initiation of faith, not its continuation or permanence.
key_phrases: the Lord opened her heart to pay attention

sections.section_title: The Slave Girl with the Spirit of Python
sections.summary: A slave girl with a spirit of divination follows the missionaries proclaiming them 'servants of the Most High God who proclaim the way of salvation' -- factually accurate words from a false source; Paul, greatly annoyed, commands the spirit to come out in Jesus's name.

sections.section_title: Economic Loss, False Charges, and Imprisonment
sections.summary: The slave girl's owners, their revenue destroyed, drag Paul and Silas before the magistrates on fabricated charges of promoting unlawful customs; they are beaten with rods and thrown into the inner prison with feet in stocks.

sections.section_title: Prayer, Earthquake, and the Opened Prison
sections.summary: At midnight Paul and Silas pray and sing hymns while prisoners listen; an earthquake opens all doors and unfastens all bonds; Paul prevents the jailer's suicide by calling out 'We are all here.'

sections.section_title: The Jailer's Question and Household Conversion
sections.summary: The jailer asks 'What must I do to be saved?'; Paul and Silas answer 'Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household'; the word of the Lord is spoken to the entire household, the jailer washes their wounds, he and his household are baptized immediately, and 'he rejoiced along with his entire household that he had believed in God.'
sections.relevance: The soteriological formula 'Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved' (v. 31) presents salvation as a direct consequence of believing, with no additional conditions mentioned. The future passive 'you will be saved' (sothese) presents salvation as a certain outcome of belief. The promise extends to the household. The neutral reading notes that the perfect participle pepisteukos ('having believed') describes the jailer's faith as 'a completed action with ongoing effect -- he has believed and continues in that belief.' However, the passage does not address what happens if belief ceases; it presents the positive sequence (believe -> be saved) without discussing the negative possibility.
key_phrases: Believe in the Lord Jesus and you will be saved
having believed -- a completed action with ongoing effect

sections.section_title: Roman Citizenship and the Magistrates' Fear
sections.summary: Paul reveals his Roman citizenship, demands a public acknowledgment of wrongdoing from the magistrates who beat them illegally, receives their personal apology and escort, and visits Lydia's house to encourage the brothers before departing.
